array_aliasing.quote: 1; b is a copy of a; so changing b[0] doesnt touch a
array_aliasing.rule: wrong rule: Assigning an array reference copies the array. Right rule: b = a; copies only the reference, so a and b refer to the same array and b[i] = v also changes a[i].

paths.label: held
paths.quote: 1; b is a copy of a; so changing b[0] doesnt touch a
paths.logic: assigning a reference copies the object
paths.twin_logic: b = a; copies only the reference, so a and b refer to the same array and b[i] = v also changes a[i].

paths.label: shown
paths.quote: 1; b is a copy of a; so changing b[0] doesnt touch a
paths.logic: Folk meaning: in maths and English, 'b = a' means b becomes an equal but independent copy, and 'a == b' means 'have the same values'. Java rule: for arrays, b = a copies only the reference, so both names denote one array, and == tests whether two names refer to the same array.

paths.label: shown
paths.logic: Result: int[] a = {1, 2, 3}; gives a.length == 3, a[0] == 1, a[2] == 3. String[] suit = {"Clubs", "Diamonds", "Hearts", "Spades"}; gives suit.length == 4.

paths.label: broken
paths.quote: 1; b is a copy of a; so changing b[0] doesnt touch a
paths.logic: Because an array variable holds a reference, b = a copies the reference, so a and b name the same array.

paths.label: confirmed
paths.logic: The values listed in braces are stored at indices 0, 1, 2, ... in order, and a[i] reads the value at index i.

paths.label: shown
paths.quote: 1; b is a copy of a; so changing b[0] doesnt touch a
paths.logic: Folk meaning: a variable is a box, so the array's values are 'inside' a. Java rule: the variable a holds only a reference (memory address, pointer) to the array object, which lives elsewhere.
